text: Lesson 30 gave Caldwell's incidents a real Priority. This lesson is where that Priority, and every other stakeholder ask still open, becomes something provable instead of a promise.

SLA Definitions get built one per priority tier. Priority 1, tied to a Meridian outage, gets a one-hour response and four-hour resolution target running twenty-four seven, no schedule attached, because a company-wide outage doesn't pause for the weekend. Priority 2 runs against an eight-to-five weekdays schedule instead. Every definition's Start condition fires on State equals In Progress, not on creation, so queue time doesn't eat into the target, and Pause suspends the clock during Awaiting Caller so a slow callback doesn't burn the team's own window.

HR's new-hire catalog item generates one sc_request and two sc_req_item records: one for the laptop and standard image, one for ERP and VPN access. Each gets its own SLA, because the provisioning team and the access-approval team run on genuinely different timelines. The Request's own state rolls up from its items, so if the laptop is done but access isn't, the request shows a calculated Partially Complete instead of closing early or looking stuck.

The service desk supervisor's complaint gets solved with a real Knowledge Base, not a shared document nobody updates. Articles on password reset, VPN setup, and submitting a New Hire request go through Draft, a designated reviewer, and Publication before anyone relies on them, and an article tied to the old Line 3 symptom gets flagged for retirement once the switch is actually replaced, instead of quietly misleading the next agent who searches for it. A single Service Portal widget, My Open Requests, queries sc_request filtered to the current user, so any employee can check their own order's status without calling the desk at all.
Every row from Lesson 29's checklist is now real configuration. Lesson 32 closes the capstone by mapping everything Caldwell just got built back to the CIS-ITSM certification's own domain areas.
